annotations.ui_text:
Set the mode you want to use and it's appropriate parameters:
 - Letterbox: Displays bars on the image to 'correct' aspect ratio.
 - Test Box: Displays a box in the center of the screen representing the selected aspect ratio.
 - Multi-Test Box: Same as Test Box but shows multiple boxes from aspect ratios defined in the ASPECT_RATIO_SUITE_VALUES macro.

The macro for Multi-Test Box mode is defined as a comma-separated list of aspect ratios, which can be defined as the division of two decimal numbers.

For example, '4.0 / 3.0, 16.0 / 9.0, 1.0', would tell the effect to display boxes for 4:3, 16:9 and 1:1 aspect ratios.

For short-handing, you could also define the same values as '4/3., 16/9., 1', since you only need one of the numbers in the division to be decimal and it's decimal places can be omitted.

Remember you can also pass the mouse cursor over a parameter's name to see a more detailed description and it's default value.

RadiantGI is an indirect lighting algorithm based on the disk-to-disk radiance transfer by Michael Bunnell.
As you can tell its name is a play on words and it radiates the kind of feeling I want from it one Ray Bounce at a time.
This GI shader is free and shouldn't sit behind a paywall. If you paid for this shader ask for a refund right away.
As for my self I do want to provide the community with free shaders and any donations will help keep that motivation alive.
For more information and help please feel free to visit http://www.Depth3D.info or https://blueskydefender.github.io/AstrayFX
 Help with this shader fuctions specifically visit the WIki @ https://github.com/BlueSkyDefender/AstrayFX/wiki/RadiantGI

This effect allows you to overwrite the transparency of screenshots using the scene depth as the alpha channel.

You'll need a version of ReShade with the option to disable "Clear Alpha Channel" in the screenshot settings.

If you use a different key for taking screenshots, it may be useful to change the value of DEPTH_ALPHA_SCREENSHOT_KEY to something other than VK_SNAPSHOT (the keycode for the printscreen key).

To see which keycodes are available, refer to the "KeyCodes.fxh" file in the FXShaders repository shaders folder.

annotations.ui_tooltip:
Defines the depth range for the depth multipliers.
 - The first value defines the start of the middle depth. - The second value defines the end of the middle depth and the start of the far depth.
Default: 0.0 1.0

Multipliers for the transparency of near, middle and far depth respectively.
Set to 0.0 to make a range completely transparent, 1.0 to make it completely opaque.

Default: 1.0 0.5 0.0

Smoothness of the transitions between depth multiplier ranges.

Default: 1.0

Determines whether the effect should reset the alpha of the image to100% opaque before applying the effect or maintain it (applying the effect over the previous alpha).

Default: Off

Preview transparency by colorizing it.
This option is automatically disabled when the key defined in DEPTH_ALPHA_SCREEENSHOT_KEY is being held down, which is the printscreen key by default.
There's a small chance that the test color might still appear in the screenshot, but keeping the screenshot key held for a small time seems to help.
You can also simply disable this option before taking a screenshot.

Default: Off

The color used when Colorize Transparency is enabled.
The alpha channel of this color has nothing to do with the final result, it merely serves to determine the opacity of this color while testing.

Default: 0 0 0 255
The strength of the effect. Range from 0.0, which means no effect, till 1.0 which means pixels are 100% blurred based on depth.

This effect allows you to add both bloom and tonemapping, drastically changing the mood of the image.

annotations.ui_text:
NeoBloom has many options and may be difficult to setup or may look bad at first, but it's designed to be very flexible to adapt to many different cases.
Make sure to take a look at the preprocessor definitions at the bottom!
For more specific descriptions, move the mouse cursor over the name of the option you need help with.

Here's a general description of the features:

  Bloom:
    Basic options for controlling the look of bloom itself.

  Adaptation:
    Used to dynamically increase or reduce the image brightness depending on the scene, giving an HDR look.
    Looking at a bright object, like a lamp, would cause the image to darken; lookinng at a dark spot, like a cave, would cause the image to brighten.

  Blending:
    Used to control how the different bloom textures are blended, each representing a different level-of-detail.
    Can be used to simulate an old mid-2000s bloom, ambient light etc.

  Ghosting:
    Smoothens the bloom between frames, causing a "motion blur" or "trails" effect.

  Depth:
    Used to increase or decrease the brightness of parts of the image depending on depth.
    Can be used for effects like brightening the sky.
    An optional anti-flicker feature is available to help with games with depth flickering problems, which can cause bloom to flicker as well with the depth feature enabled.

  HDR:
    Options for controlling the high dynamic range simulation.
    Useful for simulating a more foggy bloom, like an old soap opera, a high-contrast sunny look etc.

  Blur:
    Options for controlling the blurring effect used to generate the bloom textures.
    Mostly can be left untouched.

  Debug:
    Enables testing options, like viewing the bloom texture alone, before mixing with the image.

annotations.ui_tooltip:
Determines how much bloom is added to the image. For HDR games you'd generally want to keep this low-ish, otherwise everything might look too bright.

Default: 1.0

Saturation of the bloom texture.

Default: 1.0

Color multiplied to the bloom, filtering it.
Set to full white (255, 255, 255) to disable it.

Default: 255 255 255

Determines the formula used to blend bloom with the scene color.
Certain blend modes may not play well with other options.
As a fallback, addition always works.

Default: Mix

Acts as a bias between all the bloom textures/sizes. What this means is that lower values will yield more detail bloom, while the opposite will yield big highlights.
The more variance is specified, the less effective this setting is, so if you want to have very fine detail bloom reduce both parameters.

Default: 0.0

Determines the 'variety'/'contrast' in bloom textures/sizes. This means a low variance will yield more of the bloom size specified by the mean; that is to say that having a low variance and mean will yield more fine-detail bloom.
A high variance will diminish the effect of the mean, since it'll cause all the bloom textures to blend more equally.
A low variance and high mean would yield an effect similar to an 'ambient light', with big blooms of light, but few details.

Default: 1.0

tl;dr: HDR contrast.

Determines the maximum brightness a pixel can achieve from being 'reverse-tonemapped', that is to say, when the effect attempts to extract HDR information from the image.
In practice, the difference between a value of 100 and one of 1000 would be in how bright/bloomy/big a white pixel could become, like the sun or the headlights of a car.
Lower values can also work for making a more 'balanced' bloom, where there are less harsh highlights and the entire scene is equally foggy, like an old TV show or with dirty lenses.

Default: 100.0

Whether to normalize the bloom brightness when blending with the image.
Without it, the bloom may have very harsh bright spots.

Default: On

When enabled, simulates the look of MagicBloom.
This is an experimental option and may be inconsistent with other parameters.

Default: Off

Amount of blurriness. Values too high will break the blur.
Recommended values are between 2 and 4.

Default: 2.0

Specifies additional padding around the bloom textures in the internal texture atlas, which is used during the blurring process.
The reason for this is to reduce the loss of bloom brightness around the screen edges, due to the way the blurring works.

If desired, it can be set to zero to purposefully reduce the amount of bloom around the edges.
It may be necessary to increase this parameter when increasing the blur sigma, samples and/or bloom down scale.

Due to the way it works, it's recommended to keep the value as low as necessary, since it'll cause the blurring process to work in a "lower" resolution.

If you're still confused about this parameter, try viewing the texture atlas with debug mode and watch what happens when it is increased.

Default: 0.1
